description: Named after the Australian emergency dispatch code, 000 Orbital Triage is a specialized two-person team dedicated to deep-space medical software. Returning to the NASA Space Apps Challenge after tackling space bioscience risk data in previous years, we bring a unique blend of enterprise systems architecture and creative operations to the 2026 health monitoring challenge.
summary:
When a medical crisis occurs halfway to Mars, a 12-minute communication delay means astronauts cannot wait for Houston’s orders. Because astronauts are not doctors, they need immediate, actionable direction—not raw biological data.

To solve this, Team 000 Orbital Triage developed BioTriage Explorer, a cross-platform emergency health application. Functioning like an IT incident response system for human biology, our prototype ingests wearable telemetry utilizing NASA’s Open Science Data Repository (OSDR) data structures. When vital signs breach NASA Human Research Program (HRP) thresholds, the system instantly triggers a progressive, high-contrast triage workflow. It dynamically adapts to the operational environment (Spacecraft, Lunar Base) to guide non-medical crew members through precise sensor placement, medication administration, and patient stabilization before initiating a delayed Houston uplink.

This project is critical for deep-space survivability, closing the medical knowledge gap during communications blackouts. Crucially, our architecture scales directly to Earth, empowering bystanders to stabilize patients in remote, isolated environments like the Australian Outback while awaiting emergency medical services.
details:
What It Does & How It Works BioTriage Explorer is a cross-platform emergency health application that translates complex biological telemetry into an actionable, high-contrast triage workflow. Instead of overwhelming non-medical crew members with raw data graphs, the app functions like an IT Service Management (ITSM) incident responder for human biology.

The workflow is broken into three foolproof stages:

  1. Context & Ingest: The user selects their operational environment (Spacecraft, Space Station, or Lunar Base) and confirms biosensor placement through a progressive disclosure UI.
  2. Dynamic Intervention: Using mock JSON data modeled after NASA’s Open Science Data Repository (OSDR), the app ingests telemetry. If NASA Human Research Program (HRP) thresholds are breached (e.g., 135 BPM HR / 92% SpO2), a high-contrast emergency checklist is triggered. This checklist dynamically adapts to the environment (e.g., adding "Lunar Dust Mitigation" protocols for Moon Bases).
  3. Houston Hand-Off: Once the patient is stabilized, the system initiates a deep-space uplink, explicitly simulating the ~12-minute speed-of-light ping delay between Mars and Earth, giving the crew a clear system status while they wait for ground control.

Creativity & Factors Considered We recognized a critical flaw in current space medicine dashboards: they assume the user is a doctor. In a high-stress medical emergency halfway to Mars, cognitive load is a massive factor. We prioritized "massive affordances" in our UI/UX design. We discarded text-heavy manuals and web-blocking pop-ups in favor of a clean, dark-mode card layout with scannable emojis, strict sequential locks (disabling buttons until previous steps are confirmed), and integrated on-screen alerts. We considered the extreme psychological isolation of deep space, designing the system to act as a calm, authoritative digital medical officer.

Intended Impact & Benefits The primary benefit is enabling immediate, confident medical intervention during deep-space communication blackouts, directly increasing crew survivability. Crucially, the intended impact extends back to Earth. This exact architecture scales seamlessly to remote, isolated environments—like the Australian Outback. By translating complex vitals into simple actions, we empower rural bystanders to stabilize patients while the Royal Flying Doctor Service or regional paramedics are en route.

Tools, Languages, & Software Used We leveraged a modern, cross-platform mobile and web stack to ensure the application could run on any tablet or terminal:

  • Frontend Framework: React Native and Expo. We overrode Expo's default SSR settings, utilizing the Metro bundler to export a lightweight Single Page Application (SPA).
  • Navigation: React Navigation (Native Stack) for seamless, state-preserved screen transitions.
  • Languages: JavaScript (ES6+), JSX, and CSS-in-JS (React Native StyleSheet).
  • Version Control & CI/CD: Git, GitHub, and Vercel for live, continuous deployment of our web-compatible build.
  • Data Architecture: Custom JSON payloads modeled strictly after NASA OSDR assay structures (Electrocardiography, Pulse Oximetry, Dosimetry).
  • Design & Media: Canva Pro and Canva AI were heavily utilized for UI ideation, generating presentation collateral, and recording the final pitch video over a live screen-share. Visual Studio Code served as our primary IDE.

Future Prospects Due to the strict time limits of this rapid hackathon sprint, we focused entirely on UI/UX perfection and simulated telemetry. Moving forward, our roadmap includes:

  1. Hardware Integration: Replacing the mock OSDR JSON with real-time Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) ingestion from commercial wearables (e.g., Garmin, Apple Watch).
  2. AI-Driven Diagnostic Branching: Implementing a lightweight, on-device Local LLM that can dynamically adjust triage protocols based on compounding, multi-system symptoms.
  3. Offline-First Synchronization: Integrating a local database (like SQLite/WatermelonDB) for persistent medical log storage that automatically syncs with Houston the moment a communication window opens.
dataRefs: NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR) - We utilized the OSDR biological assay data structures as the architectural model for our application's telemetry ingest. Specifically, we modeled our mock JSON payloads (used during the prototype's live scan phase) on OSDR standard formats for Electrocardiography (ECG), Pulse Oximetry, and Dosimetry to ensure our software can seamlessly integrate with real NASA datasets in the future.

NASA Human Research Program (HRP) - We referenced the Human Research Program's physiological parameters to establish the critical baseline thresholds for deep-space vital signs. The medical triggers in our triage workflow (such as a 135 BPM heart rate and a drop to 92% SpO2) were modeled against HRP spaceflight adaptation risks to ensure the app's alerts reflect realistic deep-space medical events.
projectRefs: React Native - Used as the core frontend framework to build the cross-platform triage interface, utilizing JavaScript, JSX, and React Native StyleSheet to ensure the UI scales perfectly across tablets, mobile devices, and web browsers.
Expo - Utilized for rapid project scaffolding, local development serving, and configuring
React Navigation - Implemented the Native Stack navigator library to manage seamless, state-preserved screen routing between the three core phases of our app
Vercel - Employed as our cloud hosting and deployment platform.
GitHub - Served as our primary version control system and open-source code repository
Canva Pro & Canva AI - Utilised for Video editing
Visual Studio Code (VS Code) - Served as our primary Integrated Development Environment (IDE) for writing, formatting, and debugging the JavaScript codebase.
